newsitem.title: CHINA: HK families surrender illegal migrant children.
newsitem.headline: HK families surrender illegal migrant children.

text.p: Hundreds of families flocked to Hong Kong's immigration headquarters on Friday to surrender illegal immigrant children who had sneaked in from China, hoping they would be allowed to stay and obtain residency rights.
The rush was sparked by a pronouncement on Thursday that child illegals could remain here while their parental background was checked to determine if they had a right to stay.
Families who have been hiding mainland-born children smuggled in from China clearly interpreted the pronouncement as a virtual amnesty and "touch base" policy.
"We came to get permission for my daughter to stay," said Lo Chui-yuk, mother of seven-year-old illegal Cheng Chi-man.
"I like staying in Hong Kong where mummy can take care of me," said Cheng, whose parents are both Hong Kong residents.
Other young illegal immigrants were equally eager to stay.
"It'll be sad if I'm separated from my father," said seven-year-old Lam Ting-ting, who was smuggled in six years ago.
The Immigration Department set up a special office in its main lobby to cope with the avalanche of cases from a queue that started to form at dawn.
"I came early because I thought there might be over 1,000 people coming," said the father of another young illegal, who had waited at the department since Thursday night.
On Thursday the authorities said child illegals would not be repatriated immediately if they could prove they have residency rights under Hong Kong's new constitution, the Basic Law.

The constitution, which took effect on Tuesday when the former British colony became a quasi-autonomous Chinese territory, says mainland-born offspring of a Hong Kong permanent resident are entitled to stay here.

But under current arrangements, they must apply to Chinese authorities for permission to migrate to Hong Kong, which can mean a wait of years as only 150 Chinese immigrants, 66 of them children, are allowed into the territory daily.
"It's not fair that the children cannot live here. The Basic Law says they have residency rights here," said Lam's father.
Some parents complained about the procedures in China.
"The Chinese authorities haven't approved my daughter's coming here. There's much corruption in China," Lo said.

Adult illegals and overstayers, mostly parents of young illegals, also arrived to give themselves up, in the belief that they too might qualify for residency status under some kind of general amnesty.

"China has never allowed us to apply for coming as immigrants. We hope Hong Kong will let us apply here directly," said a 25-year-old overstayer, daughter of a Hong Kong resident, who has been in the territory for four years.
"I feel there is freedom and human rights in Hong Kong. China doesn't even give us the rights we should have," she said.
But the immigration authorities were taking a firm line on some of these people, prosecuting about 30 overstayers who turned themselves in on Friday.
Immigration officer Leung Ping-kwan said 10 illegal immigrants would be deported.
"Those who do not qualify to stay will be deported right away," an immigration official told the queue through loudspeakers.

Secretary for Security Peter Lai reiterated that there would be no amnesty. "I hope nobody will misunderstand that there's a special arrangement for illegal immigrants to stay in Hong Kong or any kind of amnesty action," he said.
"Our police and Chinese police authorities will also strengthen patrols at the border," he said.
Administrative Secretary Anson Chan said the government would "very soon" announce how the government is to handle Chinese illegal immigrants claiming residency rights in Hong Kong.
It is estimated that 60,000 children from "separated families" are waiting to settle in the territory.
